Title: 68881/68882: FMOVE to memory or Dn takes a mid-instruction exception

---

On a 68020 or 68030 with a 68881 or 68882, an `FMOVE FPn,<ea>` to memory or to a data register that raises an enabled exception stores the operand and records the exception. Master takes it later, as a pre-instruction exception, when the next FPU instruction starts. For example, `FMOVE.L FP0,(A0)` of +infinity with OPERR enabled, followed by `FNOP`: master writes `$7FFFFFFF` to (A0), executes the FMOVE without trapping, and the FNOP then stacks a format $0 frame with vector 52 and the address of the FNOP. The handler cannot see which instruction raised the exception or where the result went, except through FPIAR.

The 6888x manual reports this exception from inside the FMOVE: "FPCP instruction exceptions that arise from the move floating-point data register to external destination instructions are reported to the MPU as mid-instruction exceptions" [MC68881UM §6.1](https://www.nxp.com/docs/en/reference-manual/MC68881UM.pdf#page=228), and "a take mid-instruction exception primitive is issued after the operand is stored in memory (if a conversion error occurred)" [§6.1](https://www.nxp.com/docs/en/reference-manual/MC68881UM.pdf#page=226). The dialog description says the same: "The MC68881 uses this dialog only if an exception occurs during the execution of the FMOVE FPm,<ea> instruction. In this case, the protocol for the normal execution of the instruction is followed, and then the mid-instruction exception is reported with the last primitive (in lieu of the null primitive normally used to terminate the dialog)" [§7.5.4.2](https://www.nxp.com/docs/en/reference-manual/MC68881UM.pdf#page=296).

For OPERR: "For memory or MPU data register destinations, the destination operand is written as if the trap were disabled, and then a take exception primitive is returned to the MPU. This can only occur for the FMOVE FPm,<ea> instruction, and the exception is reported as a mid-instruction exception" [§6.1.3](https://www.nxp.com/docs/en/reference-manual/MC68881UM.pdf#page=232). §6.1.2 (SNAN), §6.1.4 (OVFL), §6.1.5 (UNFL) and §6.1.7 (INEX2) say the same for a memory or MPU data register destination. Their sentences about a pre-instruction exception reported when the next floating-point instruction is attempted concern a floating-point register destination. These are the five exceptions a move-out can raise. DZ, INEX1 and BSUN come from other instructions.

The frame is the ten-word mid-instruction frame of [§7.4.2.6](https://www.nxp.com/docs/en/reference-manual/MC68881UM.pdf#page=282) and [Figure 7-16](https://www.nxp.com/docs/en/reference-manual/MC68881UM.pdf#page=283), MC68020UM §7.4.19 (Figure 7-43) and MC68030UM §10.4.19 (Figure 10-43): "If the exception is due to an FMOVE FPn,<ea> instruction, the ScanPC value is the address of the instruction immediately following the FMOVE instruction. The value of the program counter in the stack frame is the address of the F-line operation word of the FPCP instruction that caused the exception. The operation word image contains the F-line word of the FMOVE instruction. The effective address value is the memory address of the destination operand."

What changes:
- `execFMove` takes the exception right after the store on the 6888x, as it already did on the 68040.
- `writeStackFrame1001` (an empty stub on master) writes the frame: SR at +$00, scan PC at +$02, `1001 | vector offset` at +$06, the FMOVE's address at +$08, the internal register at +$0C, the operation word at +$0E and the effective address at +$10. The manuals do not say what the internal register holds, so it is written as 0. For a data register destination, MC68030UM §10.4.19 (and MC68020UM §7.4.19): "If the current instruction does not evaluate an effective address prior to the exception request primitive, the value of the effective address field in the stack frame is undefined." I read this as covering a data register destination; Moira writes 0 there.
- `execFpuTrap` picks format 3 on the 68040 and format 9 on the 6888x. The 68040 path is unchanged.
- `execFpuTrap` no longer clears a pending trace for the format 9 case (see Trace below).

RTE needed no change: `readRteFrame68020` already reads format $9 (20 bytes) and reloads the PC from +$02, the scan PC. On the chip the processor then reads the response CIR (MC68030UM §8.1.13). The 68881 answers with a null primitive: "Since the MC68881 always finishes execution of the instruction that causes this type of exception before reporting it, the response that is returned is null (CA=0, PF = 1), which releases the main processor to continue with the execution of the next instruction" [§6.1.13](https://www.nxp.com/docs/en/reference-manual/MC68881UM.pdf#page=247).

Trace. On master, a traced FMOVE completes and is traced, and the exception comes later. With this change, the exception is taken inside the FMOVE, so the order of the two exceptions has to be chosen. I kept the pending trace and let it be processed right after the format $9 frame, before the first instruction of the handler. That is the order the 68020 core already uses for TRAP, CHK, TRAPV and divide by zero. MC68030UM §8.1.7: "If an instruction forces an exception as part of its normal execution, the forced exception processing occurs before the trace exception is processed", and Table 8-6 lists "cp Mid-Instruction" in group 2 ("Exception processing is part of instruction execution") with TRAP, and the trace in group 4. This is not proven; the alternative is in "Not covered".

One existing assertion block changes. In `FpuExecTests.cpp`, the `"68882"` subcase of "FMOVE to memory raises a post-instruction exception on the 68040" ran `FMOVE.L FP0,(A0); FNOP` for two instructions and expected the FNOP to stack a format 0 frame (`read16(sp + 6) == 52 * 4`) with the FNOP's address at +2. That is the deferred behaviour quoted above as wrong. The subcase now runs only the FMOVE and expects the FPU handler, format 9 (`0x9000 | 52 * 4`), the scan PC (`codeStart + 4`) at +2, the FMOVE's address at +8, the operation word `$F210` at +$0E, the effective address `$2000` at +$10 and nothing left pending. The +2 value it already checked, `codeStart + 4`, is unchanged; it is now the scan PC, not the address of the FNOP. I left the subcase in its test case, next to the 68040 subcase it contrasts with, so that only these assertions change; the FNOP stays in the program to show that the exception is no longer deferred to it. The comment above the arithmetic exception tests is updated. The comment on the UAE skip rule in `Tests/Random/UAERef.cpp` also said Moira defers the exception; it is updated too, and the rule itself is unchanged.

New test case "FMOVE to memory or to a data register raises a mid-instruction exception on the 6888x". A helper checks, for every format $9 frame: the handler, SP (20 bytes below the supervisor stack), the stacked SR, the scan PC, the format and vector, the FMOVE's address, the operation word, FPIAR and that nothing is left pending. The internal register is not checked.
- SNAN, OPERR, OVFL, UNFL and INEX2, each on the 68020 and 68030 with a 68881 and a 68882, to (A0) and to D1: the stored result equals the one written with the exception disabled (the destination is pre-filled with `$FFFFFFFF`), the full frame, and the effective address for (A0). The effective address is not checked for D1.
- Addressing modes, 68020 and 68030: `(A0)`, `(A0)+` (EA is the old A0, A0 incremented), `-(A0)` (EA is the decremented A0), `($10,A0)` (scan PC +6) and `($3000).L` (scan PC +8): the stored value, A0, the frame and the effective address.
- An `FMOVE.X FP0,FP1` of a signaling NaN still leaves FP1 unchanged and the exception pending (§6.1, §6.1.2). This subcase checks unchanged behaviour and passes on master too.
- RTE, on the 68020 and 68030, from supervisor mode (SR $2700) and from user mode (SR $0700, the frame then holds $0700), with a 68881 and a handler that is a bare RTE: the handler runs before the instruction after the FMOVE (an ADDQ); the RTE returns to that ADDQ (the scan PC, not the FMOVE at +$08) with SR and SP restored; the following FNOP does not trap again.
- A traced FMOVE (SR $A700), 68020 and 68030: the format $9 frame holds SR $A700; the next step takes the trace exception before the handler's first instruction: PC at the trace vector, a format $2 frame 12 bytes below the format $9 frame, with SR $2700, the address of the FPU handler as the next instruction, `$2024` and the FMOVE's address as the instruction address.

With the test changes alone on master (bf98107), 501 of 1037 assertions in the FPU tests fail: all seven of the updated `"68882"` subcase's, and those of four of the five new subcases (all but the floating-point register one). With the change, the FPU tests pass (1037 assertions), as do `unit` (6240) and `unitfast` (30). `randomuae --seed 1 --cpu 68030 --fpu 68881 --fpu 68882` passes. The full `ctest` passes on this commit (26/26, including RandomUAE, the SequenceUAE runs and ExceptionUAE020).

Not covered:
- Trace, the alternative reading. The coprocessor sections favour taking the trace after the handler's RTE, when the FMOVE's dialog ends. MC68030UM §10.4.4 (MC68020UM §7.4.4 has the same text): "If a trace exception is pending, however, the main processor does not terminate the instruction dialogue until it reads a null, CA=0, PF=1 primitive from the response CIR (refer to 10.5.2.5 TRACE EXCEPTIONS). Thus, the main processor continues to read the response CIR until it receives a null, CA=0, PF=1 primitive, and then performs trace exception processing." §10.4.19: after the handler, "the main processor attempts to continue executing the suspended instruction by reading the response CIR and processing the primitive it receives". §10.5.2.5: "When a trace exception is pending, however, the main processor must ensure that all processing associated with a cpGEN instruction has been completed before it takes the trace exception." MC68881UM §7.4.2.6: "If no modifications are made to the stack frame within the exception handler, an RTE instruction causes the MPU to return to read the response CIR." §8.1.7 itself defers the trace of an instruction suspended by a bus or address error until "the instruction execution completes normally", and even §8.1.4 says of instruction traps that "a trace exception is taken after the RTE instruction from the trap handler is executed". Against that stand §8.1.7's sentence on forced exceptions and Table 8-6 quoted above, and the example in §8.1.12 (trap, then trace, then the trace handler runs first). Only a capture on a 68020 or 68030 with a 68881 settles it. If you read it the other way, I can change it to take the trace after the RTE. Trace on change of flow (T0) is not handled for this exception: unlike TRAP, it does not set a trace.
- The 68882 does not clear the exception on the acknowledge: "When the exception handler does not contain an FSAVE instruction, the take mid-instruction exception primitive is not replaced by a null primitive, and the next floating-point instruction takes the exception again" [§7.5.4.2](https://www.nxp.com/docs/en/reference-manual/MC68881UM.pdf#page=299). For the concurrent case with a handler that omits the BSET, the next paragraph has the main processor re-read the primitive right after the RTE: "Following the return from the exception handler, the main processor reads the take mid-instruction exception primitive from the response CIR and performs exception processing again for the same exception" (Figure 7-35). Moira takes it once on both FPUs, as it already does for the pre-instruction exceptions. A 68882 handler that follows §5.2.2 (FSAVE, BSET of bit 27, FRESTORE, RTE) is not affected. The UAE copy keeps the exception pending on the 68882 (`fp_exception_pending` in `Tests/ThirdParty/UAE/src/fpp.cpp`).
- UAE agrees on the timing: it takes the exception right after the store (`fp_exception_pending(false)` after the move-out in `fpp.cpp`). It differs on the frame: it stacks format $3 (`Exception_build_stack_frame_common` in `newcpu_common.cpp`), a format the 68020 and 68030 do not have. `UAERef::skipSetup` already skips an FMOVE-out with any exception enabled on these FPUs, so no differential test compares this case. SequenceUAE runs without an FPU.
- The internal register at +$0C is written as 0.
- A 68882 can also report an exception of an earlier, concurrent instruction as a mid-instruction exception of a later one (§6.1, §7.5.4.2). Moira still reports those as pre-instruction exceptions.
- No cycles are charged for the exception, as on the 68040 path.
